items.body: For more than two decades, IAMX, the solo project of artist Chris Corner, has occupied a singular, ineffable space within dark and alternative music, while at the same time managing to bend and penetrate genres outside the scene. IAMX returns to Europe this summer for the Recollections Tour, with special appearances at festivals including M’era Luna, Infest, and Extramuralhas, alongside a run of headline dates across more unusual territories, including the Nordic countries, Türkiye, and others to be confirmed. Fans can find tickets to all shows on the IAMX website. A highlight of the run is a double-night invasion of Stockholm. The band will perform their infamous, electrifying, high-octane set one night, while also offering a super unique acoustic set and mental health gathering on another. Set against a backdrop of high-art stage design and bombastic rave visuals, the main set will include revamped beloved IAMX classics not heard for years, along with heavier live versions of recent albums. Held the evening before, the acoustic gathering offers honest conversations about mental health, neurodiversity, and sexuality, interwoven with stripped-back acoustic performances of IAMX songs. Ahead of their first shows, Corner and IAMX live band member Gözde Düzer, known for her own fantastic, gritty hauntwave solo project Aux Animaux, turn the spotlight on one another for their own intimate conversation over a few glasses of wine. Their discussion travels from the evolution of IAMX to mental health and neurodiversity, and finding connection in an increasingly fractured world. Photo by Kris Sulekova Gözde: After a period of intense focus on the Fault Lines era, we’re going to be doing this tour focused a bit more on older songs. How does it feel to move into a retrospective realm? Chris: It feels bizarre and amazing at the same time. I felt like the Fault Lines thing dragged on, really, because a lot of personal stuff dragged on. What was happening in my personal life and those two albums seemed so intertwined with each other that they both felt like the same thing in an odd way. Moving into this retrospective thing, I am ready to write new material, but not quite. My head is still stuck on a personal level. I’m trying to shake myself up, and I think doing this retrospective thing gives me a bit of breathing space, but also allows me to be playful with old stuff and have some fun and give people what they want, and not be too serious. Because writing is serious. If I start fully going into the writing mode right now, I think it would just probably be too intense. There’s a certain lightness to retrospective stuff that, you know, it’s done, it’s accepted, and I can play with it and have fun with it, and not worry too much about what I’m trying to say. It’s all been said, really. It’s a bit weird, but mostly it feels perfect, timing-wise. Gözde: I think it’s also great bringing the hits to the festival shows. And also the way we play them on stage isn’t like the album version because you redo all the songs for a live performance. Everything is always being reworked in some way. One version we played in the spring might not even be the same on the stage on these summer shows, right? It’s still new and exciting. Chris: That’s part of it. Initially, it needs to be fun and cool and interesting to me. If I take an old song, I don’t want to just live with it as it was. It’s not interesting to me anymore. It’s more like, what can I do with it now, and how can I present it in a slightly more modern way? My production techniques have changed over the years, and my priorities and my sound have developed. To take an old track, I would never just do it as it was. I mean, it still has that feeling. A song is written in a certain way, you can’t extract that completely, but it is fun for me to rework it. Otherwise, I probably wouldn’t ever listen to that thing ever again. When I’ve written and produced and recorded and finished and completed and put it out, and been through the whole exposure therapy of putting art out, there’s a lot of pleasure. But there’s also a lot of self-doubt and questions. It’s never complete. I mean, that feeling, every artist has it, I’m absolutely certain. There is no perfect product. Having a second chance, that’s what I like about live stuff too, is you have many chances. You can keep improving it, and you can keep getting it better–or what you think is better, of course. Everybody has, it’s very subjective. Somebody who’s super focused on the original version of “Kiss + Swallow” from the first album might be offended by adding a new snare sound or something. I’m not. And that keeps my engine running. Gözde: That makes sense. I remember reading about Nirvana and that Kurt Cobain didn’t want to play “Smells Like Teen Spirit,” and maybe that was part of the reason why, because the album version is already super clean, and it almost doesn’t sound like that raw Nirvana sound. And then they have to play the song over and over again. But when you do something like you do, the song progresses with you, especially in a live setting, because that’s also different from the recorded version, that also keeps the song exciting for the performer too. When we play some of the IAMX songs on stage, they almost feel a bit metal. When we go all in with live drums and the bass and all… Photo by Kris Sulekova Chris: The live part of IAMX has really brought out that energy and harshness and rawness that sometimes I don’t quite achieve on the records, because my head isn’t there.When you’re making a record, you have all of these technical concerns. Your energy is very different. Your mood is different. You’re a bit more subdued, maybe. The live experience – not just for the person on stage, but for the listener, the audience too – there’s an energy that’s quite difficult to recreate in the studio. Particularly if you’re doing it yourself, like I do. You can’t always project your mind into that space, and your body, and your voice. Often it would be ideal to play the record for a whole year live and then record it, you know, like they used to do. Gözde: I think about that a lot too. Now, when I start playing the new songs live before releasing them with Aux Animaux, I realize that it was actually much better to do so, because then, even with the vocals, you come up with other stuff you wouldn’t in the studio. There’s something liberating about performing them in a live setting and then going back to the studio with whatever emerged. Chris: Exactly. And there’s a certain limit to what you can achieve in a certain time as well. You can live and breathe and experience things and see people’s reactions and see, “Oh, they like that. They don’t like that.” Or, “This worked. That worked. I felt good when I did that. My voice got stronger.” There’s too many variables. You can’t express that fully in a studio environment, particularly for the music that we do. If there’s a full band bashing away for two weeks, maybe. We’re not that. But I do love the idea of the metal energy element, and that’s something that I’m flirting with bringing into the sound, for sure. Gözde: Right! Do you mean bringing in the metal sound on the records as well? Chris: I keep coming back to this idea that there has to be an IAMX hybrid mutant metal record. I have no idea how I’ll do it, but I’ll find a way. I think it’s gonna happen. I know it. Gözde: I think it totally should! I was thinking about that the other day when I went to see the A Perfect Circle show, and then I asked you, “When are we gonna do that metal album?” Chris: I know. I come back to that feeling too. It’s odd because metal is so connected with a load of dudes on stage doing this thing. Trying to extract that energy, and formulate that into a weird electronic studio environment is a challenge. It would be really interesting if I could somehow make that. I mean, a lot of industrial stuff has that energy too. It has been done in that sense. But with IAMX it’s a different beast. Let’s see what I can do. Gözde: That’s gonna be really cool. I’m looking forward to that! By the way, going back to the highlights, “Bernadette” has exploded over the past few years to become one of the most popular IAMX songs. The single is being re-released on vinyl this summer just ahead of the tour. What do you think it is about “Bernadette” that has resonated with so many people? Chris: Obviously because it’s a really hardcore metal tune! No, it’s the least metal IAMX song ever. Who knows? I mean, there are tracks that I’ve done with different projects–my previous band–that people gravitate to. There are IAMX songs that people gravitate to. The stuff that I like is not the stuff that others like. I don’t have the answer to any of that. I’m not a pop producer or writer. I’ve never really gone into any writing process with that in mind. I’ve always found it very fragile that when people go into, at least with the people that I’ve worked with who are obviously not pop writers, when you go into that thinking, “I’m going to write a commercial song,” you’re setting yourself up for failure. I don’t know what that is. With “Bernadette,” the one thing that I remember when I wrote it, was that it was a very concentrated song. I spent a lot of time crafting it. The chord changes were very different to what I was doing at the time. I pushed things. It was a very songy-song. That’s all I can say. There’s a lot of genuine emotion in it. It’s quite simple. But then there are other IAMX songs that are simple too. I don’t know what the thing is there. It’s definitely a special song. It’s got a special thing. You can sing it like a simple song. It’s got a girl’s name. You know, the thing. It hits certain buttons that the human storytelling condition likes. You could sit around the campfire and talk about “Bernadette.” There’s a storyline to it. It has a bit of a narrative, I guess. I don’t know. Photo by Kris Sulekova Gözde: Sometimes it’s also like you just write this song from your own perspective, in your own little world, and then you put it out there for people to do whatever they want with it. And then, I guess they relate more to some songs, for reasons unknown. The song starts to have a life of its own. It makes its own path. Chris: It is on its own path. And it’s not just a relational path. It’s also a cultural path. Timing. Things that happened around it. You really can’t predict that. The only thing I can think of that has ever made any sense is when something has felt so intense and right to me that I just know it’s going to feel right to somebody else. That’s the only thing. And I have that with every song, of course. We all do. But some of those feelings last and some of them don’t. Some of them are in the moment. It’s like, “Okay, the reason why that works is because the beat was really heavy, and that feels great, and I could imagine being in a club and just losing my shit.” That’s amazing. It’s a great feeling. And it might last. But that might change next year when techno comes in, or whatever. But there’s a certain thing about a certain relational emotion that you write into a song that–I really think that if it means something true, it’s going to mean something true to somebody else. Gözde: We’ll be hosting a mental health gathering for fans with acoustic performances in August in Stockholm. It’s been several years since IAMX had a mental health gathering before a live show, and that’s going to be the first time for me doing that mental health thing with IAMX. Can you tell me a little bit about it? What is it exactly? Chris: It’s basically a safe space where we can all get in a room, be a certain accepted, weird, neurodiverse cult, and bring our challenges and our awe to the table and share it. Just talk. It’s like communion. It’s something that I know I need. It’s a selfish project, to be honest. I started it post-breakdown, when I’d had a few years of my own difficult mental health challenges. I found it super comforting and productive to start that and to do it, and to share the things that I had learned about myself, and about psychology, and therapy, and all of these tools that I had learned to restabilize myself. It was beautiful as well because it’s not just a dry therapeutic situation. It’s a very unique situation because you have an artist and the listener, and you can connect about life, but also about the art. You can go deeper into the art. I can learn things about myself, but also about them, how they experience me, how they experience my work. It’s really unique. At some point, I just felt like music, visuals, and the video, and everything, it just wasn’t enough. I was like, I’m in this world, and I’m human, and I’m socially awkward, and I don’t relate very well, but I’m desperate to relate even though I can’t. On a personal level, it’s been difficult. There were all these different moving parts. Then there’s this whole–there are thousands and thousands of people out there that accept and love me. I was like, “Well, how the fuck do I get to them on an intimate level?” Not just through social media and stuff like that. How do I sit in a room and use that energy that we both would like to use? That seemed to be a good place to do it. I’ve really missed it. It stopped for a while because life happened, and things changed, and lots of transitions, and then the pandemic happened. Here we are, five years later. It’s like, “Oh my God, I need to get back and do that shit because it was amazing.” It’s selfish, but it’s also a certain duty. One of the keys to positive and healthy mental health is to look outside yourself. To connect with others. To diminish your own ego. You can go out into nature and experience nature, and that brings your ego down. What else do you do? You get to know other people. You listen to them. You talk to them. You get to know their stories. I’m a super curious person. I love to know about others. But I need a safe environment for that because I’m also an autistic person. It’s socially sticky for me to formulate the right environment for me to do that. It’s a perfect place for me. It’s a weird corrupted social environment. Gözde: Is it because you know that they’re people who accept you as you are? That no one is judging you? Chris: In fact, it’s beyond that. It’s pure. It can be pure joy. We live in a secular world. Religion is dead to a certain degree in the Western world. And it should be, because indoctrination and dogmatic religion is horrific. Gözde: I mean, I come from Turkey, so I definitely know. Chris: Don’t get me started on that. You know. We all know the damage that dogmatic religion has done, and does, and the ignorance it creates. But, there are certain parts of our capitalist society, our culture, that has developed into a very individualist culture where we’ve lost touch with a certain sense of community. I think there are little pockets where you can still get it. This is a certain way of getting it. Through IAMX. Gözde: No, I totally get that. I was just thinking about the goth community. It’s similar, you know? Chris: Absolutely. Chris & Gözde Gözde: Since I got into the goth community, I’ve come to see they’ve been one of the sweetest, most accepting groups of people. Everyone is super nice to each other. It is a community of its own. For example, when I’m on tour and I stand by my own merch booth, you get to talk about all kinds of things with your audience. Some of them you’ve known through the years because they keep coming back. We’re going to get into talking about Patreon in a bit, where some of these people get to start communicating with you in a different way because it’s different media that can offer a closeness social media doesn’t. At the end of the day, I guess it’s similar to the closer interactions in person. I get a little bit of that from the goth scene in Stockholm, where I live, but also when I’m out traveling, and also with my little goth gang that I have in Stockholm. It’s my chosen family, as I like to call it. It’s just part of the community. The friendship. Chris: You’re absolutely right. It’s a super special, unique thing to the goth community. I don’t really see that anywhere else. It’s so accepting of vulnerability, oddness, and misfits. It’s full of people that don’t function well in society. Gözde: A lot of neurodivergent people. I think all my friends are. Chris: Exactly. Totally. We all gravitate towards that. And also the kind of music, because it’s about that stuff. I mean, that’s glorious, right? I love that. I guess this is smaller, an IAMX way of concentrating that same feeling and bringing out very specific topics, and talking specifically about people’s own experiences with neurodiversity. Advocating for openness about the whole thing. The world has got better with all of that, thankfully. It is a beautiful thing. When I started IAMX, people never talked about this stuff. Even though I’ve always put it into my music, and it’s always been there. If you look back even to the first record, you can see neurodiversity everywhere. It’s interesting to me because I wasn’t particularly aware of it myself. To be able to come full circle, and to be able to experience and share that with my people, it’s incredible. Gözde: You talked about coming out as an autistic person, and being super open, almost vulnerable, about mental health, can you tell a bit more about that? Chris: I can expand a little bit. I was late diagnosed with autism. I always felt something was very different about my place in the world, and it manifested in lots of mental health challenges. It was very freeing. It was very liberating being diagnosed because you can really start to understand yourself in a way that you never were able to. That’s a beautiful thing. You don’t necessarily have to judge yourself as a flawed, failed character. You know… Gözde: There’s even some self-acceptance, right? Chris: It really helps with self-acceptance. Gözde: Because you can say this is the way I am, and that’s okay. Chris: When you actually think about it, why do we even need neurodiversity for that? Because I guess we put it down to biology and the way our brains are structured. If my brain is structured in that way, then my consciousness and my soul, or my personality, is okay. Because, I mean, what am I anyway? Who am I? What is this thing that I call I? I’m okay then. It’s a ridiculous thing because when you actually get philosophical about it, we are everything anyway. We’re not some separate little pilot behind the eyes directing this body. There’s not a little kind of I in here taking me wherever. We are the whole thing. But there is a certain power to diagnosis. In the same way that having therapy is powerful. To understand, it’s a lifelong project. How do you truly understand the workings of your own brain? You don’t understand how your heart works, right? It just does. The brain is the most complicated thing. Why do we expect to know everything? But I think there are certain things like that that do make it a little bit smoother. Gözde: Same thing also because society is built in a certain way. Chris: Exactly. Gözde: The majority of people aren’t “wired” that way, or however you want to put it. Chris: You’re totally right. Society has a certain set of rules where, “Oh, now it can be accepted.” Because of a certain diagnosis. Because of medical expertise. That me being weird is okay in society. I think that is a really big step. It’s like racism. LGBTQ. It’s the same thing. When I got that diagnosis, it was good. It definitely helped my therapeutic journey. It explained a lot of things. It explained a lot of interpersonal issues that I thought were just moral failures that weren’t. And then being able to understand that also about my art. When I started, after the liberation of the diagnosis, understanding the things I’d written in the past. The things I’d written about, the things I’d tried to experience, the idea of me being an androgynous, pro-LGBTQ person for as long as I can remember. It all just made sense. It was quite a beautiful moment. We just expanded on it. Photo by Bianka Durcsan Gözde: I can imagine that it’s liberating in a certain way. Just understanding yourself better. Chris: It’s a lifelong battle, right? We’re all just trying to understand why we do things, how we can improve, how we can be our best selves. How we can accept ourselves. We’re instantly preoccupied with this stuff. To take quite a big chunk out of the pressure of that by saying, “Okay, well, it’s just the way I am.” I don’t have to worry about that part of me anymore. I have to align myself with it.I have to work with it. Of course that’s not going to change. Then it’s just a practical way of working. It’s not some spiritual yearning. That’s nice. It was definitely nice for me. Gözde: Maybe it even feels good to be able to say, “Okay, I’m like this.” That’s the way it is. Because now you know the reason. You can stop obsessing about certain things. Chris: Exactly. “Oh, that’s just the way I am.” It’s fine. And you can say to people, “That’s just how I am.” But you have ammunition. It’s not just, “I’m just this way.” There is a certain solidity to having a diagnosis where you can say, “Well, I am this way.” It’s not just something that I can… Gözde: It’s not something you choose. Chris: Exactly. I can’t. Gözde: Also as a touring musician, it is nice to have that diagnosis. Because we’re on the road all the time, every day we’re in a different place with different people. It’s liberating in a way also because you can say, “Okay, this is why I need certain things, because I’m an autistic person, and that’s the only way I can cope.” Chris: You just hit the nail on the head. Because I spent half my life, half my career, worrying about being an asshole. About getting a reputation for being difficult, even though I knew I couldn’t reconcile the fact that I know I’m a good person. I’m trying to be respectful to the people I work with. There are certain needs that I have that just will not go away. They aren’t negotiable. Like you’ve talked about with your misophonia. It’s not negotiable. You can’t just say, “Well, I can loosen that.” Or, “I’ll try and be a bit more like…” No, these are the needs. They have to be respected to a certain degree. They can soften, but only if you accept them, work with them, and know what they are, and others accept them too. It’s like if somebody says, “Yes, we’ll get you the quiet room in the hotel, Chris.” I’ll go, “Thank you.” Or they say, “We tried. They didn’t have one.” Okay, you tried, it’s okay. But when it’s not accepted, when it’s, “Why do you need a quiet room?” That’s a totally different ballgame. You can’t work with that. It needs to be accepted. Gözde: They definitely have more understanding when you put it that way. “Hey, this is the artist. He has autism, and that’s what we need.” I think they’re more understanding. Chris: That’s absolutely the inner feeling that changed in me post-diagnosis. That’s what I wanted to say, actually. Because pre-diagnosis, it was all like, “I am difficult. Why doesn’t anybody understand me? Why can’t I just be a bit more easygoing? Why can’t I deal with being in the noisy room? It’s just people. Why can’t I deal with that? Why can’t they just understand that I need that?” There was this constant questioning. There were so many whys. It’s all about, “Why?” And then you go, “Well, I have autism.” The “why” just dissolves. You go, “This is how it is, and we’ve got to work with it.” That sense of having to adapt to the world just falls away. It’s beautiful. You relax. I’ve actually been so much more relaxed since my diagnosis. I’ve been able to accept so much more about touring, being on the road, other people… It’s not just my own needs. I think I’ve been better to others after my diagnosis. Gözde: That’s interesting. The thing is, touring is already difficult in itself. It’s not an easy thing. People who don’t do it have no idea how tiring it is, we never sleep, we’re on the road all the time. Maybe we don’t even get to eat. You have to go out on the road, sometimes sick, and perform. Then there’s setting everything up for hours and all that work. It’s already difficult. Then there’s the part where, on top of it, you also have to meet new people every day. One of the things I really admire about you is that you’re really good at setting those boundaries for your own mental health and well-being. “This is what I need when I tour.” Because, for example, I told you about what happened to me a few weeks ago when I was on the road with Aux Animaux. I had to be in this green room with a bunch of people, take this shot with this person who insisted on it, and take a photo with another. But in reality, I was jet lagged and several days sleep deprived, all I needed was to be left alone. It’s just hard. Photo by Ghost Lens Co Chris: It is hard to say because you’re in an environment where not everybody feels like that. It’s a hyper-social environment, it’s super claustrophobic, it’s very intimate too. Backstage, the space in most places is very intimate. You’re close to people. You smell people. It’s just, for artists, especially neurodiverse people, your senses are just bombarded with intimacy. I’m not saying that you’re autistic, but I totally… Gözde: You diagnosed me as autistic, actually. Chris: I know. Gözde: I think you’re right. Definitely on the spectrum. Chris: You have special needs when you’re on the spectrum. Not a lot of people are okay with that, they don’t quite understand why. You’re in a position where you’ve just done this big thing. All of the energy has gone into the show. Then you just want to disappear, you want to go somewhere else. People think that every night’s a party, it’s not. It might be the party that night, but you’ve got another party the next night, and then another one. You don’t want to do it. Gözde: See, not everyone is partying while touring either. There’s that. But I also have friends and they’re awesome at partying on tour. Not me. I don’t do that when I tour, actually. On occasion, if I have a one-off show, or if I’m playing with friends, then whatever, but mostly I want to be left alone especially before the show. If I can’t get that, that’s a huge stress moment for me. Chris: Oh my God, yes. I totally feel you. There’s a certain sacred space before the show, right? Because you have to go inward to process what’s about to happen. Gözde: And to save your voice. Chris: Save the voice. Exactly. Save the voice. People are like, “Well, why don’t you just…” And you’re like, “Well, that’s the thing. You don’t have to do that. I do.” Gözde: Damn right! Shall we get to the next question? I want to ask you about Patreon. You were a pretty early adopter of Patreon. Inspired by you, I also got into it recently. It’s an amazing way to directly communicate with the fans. You show them what’s going on behind the scenes before everyone else sees it. It also helps us as artists financially. Has it changed anything with how you relate to your people? Chris: That was a great question. Well done. Patreon has just been a fucking lifeline for me. In a sense, I feel like IAMX could have developed it a little bit more. I feel like it’s an amazing thing that could thrive more. I want to put more energy into that. It’s a little bit like social media. I feel like Patreon is an extension of social media where I’m not… Gözde: They get something more on Patreon. Chris: They get something more. I want to be there. I want to engage. But social media is such a difficult part of the process for me. Gözde: It doesn’t feel natural, right? Chris: Not natural. Communicating is natural, creating content is natural. But this interface of going to a site, seeing something you don’t want to see, posting something, waiting for a response, there’s something so unnatural about it for me. Patreon is fucking amazing because you can throw weird, oblique stuff on there that has nothing to do with an album or an official music video. You can be playful. You can talk about stuff that has nothing to do with the main juice of the project. That’s fun. You can throw a ten-second demo of some stupid thing you’ve done, it provides content, it’s interesting, you don’t have to suffer through a social media onslaught. It’s a warmer, more intimate experience. Gözde: Because they’re curious about you, right? As a person. Chris: They’re paying. They’re specific. It’s closer. The whole thing is closer. For someone like me, it feels like a good space to experiment and experience my fans close up without it being a live experience or something like that. It’s probably the closest online to a feeling of safety that I get. Because social media is difficult for me in general. Gözde: That’s true. Social media is so broad also. On Patreon, these are the people who you know care about you, they’re rooting for you. There’s something extra going on there, definitely. Chris: Exactly. You can experiment with different formats too. You can say, “Well, I’m not good at posting this kind of content, so I’m just going to try that.” For instance, I do these voicemails. It’s just me rambling in the car, talking about life and whatever’s happening. Gözde: I totally adopted them after you. Chris: Oh, good. It’s good because it’s something I feel like I can do. It’s not forced. It’s natural. Tour Selfie Gözde: A stream of consciousness in the moment. Chris: Exactly. I’d be driving, and my head is running, and I just want to talk. I can put it out there, and people connect with it. It’s nothing to do with the way social media works. I feel like there’s a broader, more fun way to experiment there that you don’t have in other spaces. People really support you. They do it without question. They stay with you. It’s been incredible for IAMX. Gözde: I really love it too. Like I told you before, the other day, I was feeling so bad, I was crying and telling them why. Then I had people write to me saying,”I’m crying with you. I feel you.” We’re living in this world where nobody is happy all the time. On the contrary, we’re happy sometimes, here and there. But for the most part, it’s suffering. People can relate to that. I would never do that on Instagram, for example, put myself out there like that, lay myself bare. Patreon really does feel like a safe space for it. Chris: It does. It feels more authentic, right? There’s a certain thing with Instagram. There’s this constructed thing that people do. Gözde: There’s an algorithm also. Chris: There’s all of this stuff working behind the whole thing. It got worse over the years. There’s still this thing where I think…”Okay. There’s this thing I’m doing. I’m thinking. I’m feeling this thing. What do I do? Do I post that? Is that emotional porn that I want to put out into the world that’s going to make people sad? Do I want to do that?” You’re constantly thinking, “What’s right? What’s wrong?” Gözde: You know what? The part about making people sad, I don’t think that’s an issue. Because… Chris: No, I know that. It’s more that, there’s a certain clickbait kind of thing. If I do something genuinely sad or authentic, do I want to put it into a space where people think it’s clickbait anyway? It feels like the space itself is toxic. Why would I put something authentic into a toxic space? That’s what feels wrong to me sometimes. I get using it for promotion and this and that. That’s my block. Whenever I think, “This is meaningful to me.” I know it connects with my fans. But still, my post is going to sit next to some AI piece of crap that’s promoting someone shaving their head.Or, some random video. You know that your moment of depth and authenticity is just going to get lost in this stream. Gözde: I agree. But you still have to do it. As artists today we can’t just be artists who write music and perform. We have to also be content creators.You still have to do the work and be out there on social media. But I agree with you on the part that on Patreon you can share stuff that’s more intimate. It’s not about promoting. It’s about “Hey, this is right now”, and you don’t have to think about the algorithm or if this is gonna reach out, because you know the patrons are already there for it. Chris: Exactly. And it’s not gonna end up next to a toothpaste ad or something. To me whenever I’m going, it’s genuine, but then it’s next to a disgusting thing, and then I’m shocked by that thing, and I go “is that genuine?” Gözde: Totally! People’s attention span is so low because everyone’s doomscrolling all the time. Even if you put something genuine out there, it might not even be noticed. Chris: Exactly. It’s a very strange feeling. I’m blocked at this end because I know people’s attention is all over the place. Why do I post something really heartfelt about my pet dying on Instagram anymore? Or do I do it on Patreon? Anyway, back to Patreon. It just feels like a nicer, safer space to do that. I really want to work it more. Gözde: Yes. We’re going to! Chris: I’m interested in your whole experience here. You’re getting dragged along into the IAMX world. There are many moving parts: there’s the shows, there’s you playing with us as a musician in IAMX, there’s also you playing as Aux Animaux next to it. You’re experiencing the mental health gatherings. There’s a whole roller coaster here, right? What’s going on with you? How do you feel about the whole thing? Gözde: I love it. I love it so much. I’m so happy to be a part of it. I saw you many times live, before we even met. Sneaker Pimps was the soundtrack of my life back in the day. It’s still one of my favorite bands. Especially the last two albums. Chris: Exactly the right thing to say. Thank you. Gözde: It’s true, though. I just love them more because you’re singing in them, the person who actually wrote the songs, so the feeling is different. When I first got asked to play in IAMX, I did hesitate, because I was finally doing my own thing. Being my own boss. I had played with other people before, back in the day when I lived in Turkey, and the experience wasn’t great. I thought to myself, “Do I want to be in someone else’s band again when I already have something that’s going?” But then I thought, “I mean… come on. It’s IAMX. You can’t say no to that.” Thank God I didn’t. Because, we clicked right from the beginning anyway. I already knew our drummer Jon. I’m here thanks to him, actually. Then, the live experience has been phenomenal. I’m originally a bass player, it’s wonderful to get to do that again. To be in a band and not be the front person. It’s so much more fun, honestly, I enjoy it more. I’m not going to lie. Chris: I love it. I totally understand. I totally understand the feeling. The very, very few times I’ve done that… Gözde: Because you played drums, right? Chris: I played drums with an ex-girlfriend’s band. I always remember it because it was so freeing even though I was shit at it. Gözde: I’m sure you put on a hell of a performance, though. Chris: I really bashed those fucking drums. Gözde: I can imagine! Chris: I was going nuts. It was great. I enjoyed that experience of somebody else’s message, and not having to carry the whole thing. I totally understand what you’re saying. But I hope that doesn’t distract you from the amazing work that you’re doing with Aux Animaux. Gözde: No, no, no. It doesn’t. I love doing both. You know I’m working on a new album. If anything, it’s been very inspirational, it’s lovely to get to do both, actually. I get to do my own thing, but I also get to be part of this amazing project. I love everyone involved, the crew, I love being on stage with you guys. Obviously we have insane stage chemistry. I love the songs, I love the fans. Then I also have the luxury that I still get to do my own thing too. It’s just amazing. Chris: Exactly the right thing to say. Thank you. Gözde: This is different because I’m in two projects that I love. That’s awesome. I really love being a part of IAMX. Doing the support thing at the same time is, of course, a little bit difficult. I don’t get tired, it’s not about that. It’s more that I have to go on stage completely sober with Aux Animaux because I can’t play the bass when I’m drunk. That’s a little bit weird because I’m the only person on stage and everyone’s looking at me. Chris: I don’t know how you do it. Gözde: I don’t know either. It’s tough. Chris: I knew that would be, I mean, I think you’re doing an amazing job. I just thought psychologically that would be a bit of a tough call because not only do you have to psychologically shift from that person to a different person… Gözde: The shift is easy. That part is easy. Chris: It’s carrying that weight. Gözde: I mean, it’s not that it’s difficult. It’s more that it’s a little bit awkward, you’re very aware of everything, everyone. That’s a little strange. I actually used to do the shows sober up until a year or two ago. Then at some point I realized, “Oh, I can drink a little bit and then do the show.” It’s much better because then I’m more relaxed. You know? Chris: Just say it as it is. You need to be a bit loose to enjoy it. That’s part of the rock-and-roll part of it. Your project has that energy. That rock-and-roll energy needs that feeling. Not just for them, for you. You need to feel like… Gözde: Definitely. Selfie Chris: I totally understand that “being exposed” thing. There are so many layers to it. I’ve never understood those professional people who can just go on and do the show totally sober, totally straight, totally cold. Gözde: Maybe if it’s choreographed, then they can do it. But we don’t do that. We’re just rolling with our feelings at the moment. Chris: You’re right. That’s a really interesting angle. The fact that there is a certain focus to choreographed shows that occupies the mind. It takes you somewhere else. You’re focused on that thing. If you’re just about emotional, authentic energy in a way, it’s such a sterile environment. Even though gigs aren’t really built for that, it still feels sterile to suddenly jump onto a fucking platform in front of one hundred, two hundred, three hundred strangers. It’s just not natural. It doesn’t matter how many times you do it, it’s never fully natural. Gözde: That’s why it’s a little bit more difficult to do both. Because I have to be sober for IAMX. You would never know I’m sober during an IAMX show, as I probably look like I’m drunk because I have no filter then. But I am actually sober. I’m definitely more free than I even am with Aux Animaux. Maybe because I’m also a bass player, and then I’m interacting with you, another performer. Instead of standing there all alone. It’s a different thing. Chris: You’ve got technical concerns, you’ve got lighting concerns, you’ve got everything. You’re a single person on that fucking stage. It’s a big thing to carry, it really is. Super huge respect. Keep fucking doing it. Gözde: Well, we are going to do more of them now. We did the whole spring tour together like that. Then we’re going to do these Nordic shows together where I’m doing both Aux Animaux and IAMX with you. I think I’m also doing both at Extramuralhas and Infest, which isn’t on our poster because they’re festival shows. So we have two more shows together where I’m technically not stated as support because they’re festivals. Chris: You’re doing your own show, right? Gözde: I’m doing my own show on the other ones too. It’s just that those are only IAMX and Aux Animaux. Chris: It’s going to be amazing. I think. At least. Gözde: Then after that, I hope it’s just going to be only IAMX or only Aux Animaux for a little bit. Chris: It’s easier for you to do that, right? Gözde: I mean, Aux Animaux is easy. IAMX is easy and natural in any shape or form because I’m there playing the bass and interacting with you. The other one, doing both on the same night, is a little bit more tricky. Definitely. Chris: What do you have planned for Aux Animaux? Can you describe where you’re going to be in the next… This year? Five years? Sorry. Can you give me your five-year plan, please? Gözde: Haha the five year plan! This is an inside joke. Conclude the question again. Chris: No. Just, no. Gözde: Sorry. We’re getting dragged on. Chris: I think people will understand that. That would be funny. Tell me what you’re doing this year with Aux Animaux. I know you’ve described the shows. I think you told me you’re playing in the States too. Is that correct? Gözde: Yes. That is actually true. I have a whole tour planned in October. I’m playing important festivals for me, like headlining Immortalis in Portland. I’m also playing Seattle with the same festival. I’m playing Substance, both in San Francisco and Los Angeles. I’ve also got Sanctum Festival, which is very important to me, in Chicago on Halloween. Then we might have a little surprise. Other than that, I’m working on an album. Together we shot a video at your ranch in Aguanga like a month ago for the upcoming single from it. I really hope to release it sometime this summer if I can finish mixing the song.§ Chris & Gözde The conversation above follows up on an exchange Post-Punk.com began with Corner last August, ahead of IAMX’s 2025 Fault Lines² North American Tour. In that earlier interview, Corner spoke about IAMX’s first performance in New Orleans, the evolving role of Silent Valley Studios, HEADNOISE, autism, polyamory, AI’s pressure on artists and audiences, obsession as a creative engine, and the practical limits of mounting an independent tour. The discussion also reached the relationship between grief and “The Ocean,” the visual dimension of Corner’s work, and the deeper album tracks he would place on an IAMX starter mixtape. IAMX opened 2026 with “Artificial Innocence” on February 20, a new single that later appeared in two forms on the UNMASK EP: the original recording and the extended “UNMASK Mix.” Released digitally on May 22 after first being sold exclusively on the 2025 Fault Lines² European Tour, UNMASK gathers five pieces from the Fault Lines period: “Grass Before The Scythe (ArtBleedsMoney Rework),” “Artificial Innocence (UNMASK Mix),” “Radical Self Love,” “There Will Be Times When I Will Need To Hurt You,” and “Artificial Innocence.” The same day brought IAMIXED: Reworks Fault Lines Albums 1 And 2 to digital platforms after its original physical-only appearance on the 2025 North American tour. The nine-track collection hands material from both Fault Lines albums to Mimetic Hexes, Holy Braille, Damn The Witch Siren, Nigen, Carrellee, clubdrugs, and ArtBleedsMoney, and includes IAMX’s orchestral rework of “War Of Words.” On May 25, “The Background Noise {Orchestral Rework}” recast the Metanoia song in a strings-led arrangement. This summer, the Bernadette EP receives its first vinyl edition, collecting seven variations on the song, including its original recording, the ArtBleedsMoney rework, an acoustic rendition, the German radio edit, “Post Romanian Storm,” “Headfuck Collage,” and an instrumental version. Those releases now feed into the Recollections Tour, which brings earlier IAMX favorites, recent material, and newly rebuilt versions into the same set. Listen to the Bernadete EP below, and order it on vinyl here. Bernadette by IAMX The Recollections Tour begins on August 9 at M’era Luna in Hildesheim before moving to Stockholm for Intimate Conversations With IAMX on August 18 and a full-band performance at Kollektivet Livet the following night. Festival appearances at Extramuralhas in Leiria and Infest in Manchester lead into September dates through Türkiye and across southern, central, and northern Europe, including a three-night Nordic stretch in Oslo, Malmö, and Helsinki. The announced schedule concludes on November 14 with IAMX’s first performance in Brazil at Madame Club in São Paulo. Drawing from more than two decades of IAMX, the shows will place revised older songs beside recent material and special reworks. Confirmed tour dates are listed below. Tickets are available at tickets.iamxmusic.com. items.body: American boyhood can resemble a long induction into somebody else’s war. Strength is measured by the ability to make others submit; tenderness is seen as a liability; and young men learn to police one another before an employer, institution, or army ever needs to intervene. On “Victory in Death,” avant-garde darkwave project Mellow Code follows those instructions toward their brutal conclusion, confronting a model of masculinity designed to turn human beings into obedient bodies molded into the perfect vessels for capitalist greed and imperial power. Led by Josh McVety and Oliver Michael German, Mellow Code opens the track with deep, processional drums and a funereal mass of synthesizers. Buzzing, bit-crushed electronics churn across the upper register while shuddering samples keep the arrangement under strain. McVety’s resonant vocal booms from a distance, suspended somewhere between lament and military command. The track draws upon the physical machinery of early industrial music, but feels colder than EBM and graver than conventional darkwave. The body here is already bleeding out on the battlefield, with the genre’s flag lowered to half-mast. Repeated orders to “force it down” and “fall in line” turn masculinity into drill practice, while “just be a man” becomes both a taunt and a test whose only reward is further obedience. Even the title’s promised victory requires a form of self-erasure. Mellow Code explains: “Victory in death is a song evoking the feeling of growing up the way American culture targets boys. Preparation to be used as bodies for capital and imperialism. Fortify yourself little kid and don’t show weakness, that would be feminine or gay. Perpetuated in a cycle of abuse, boys police each other and the most conservative minded lash out at the perceived threats to that sense of “natural order”. Advertisements use the essence of porn and evoke rugged individualism to sell things but also that idea. The manosphere is only the newest mutant to spawn from this toxic path. These things feel inevitable at times but it’s not. Community and human contact is essential to humans, as is creating art. Sports are the most acceptable forms of community that also allow for some structured contact for young men. That’s why growing up as a soft art boy or boy adjacent can be hard. But if you’re lucky you find the other-ed and make art that speaks to rebellion against status quo gender existentialist bull shit. Maybe help some realize they also feel trapped by those structures.” Shot in the high desert, the accompanying video turns that critique into an unruly nocturnal workshop. Around a campfire, a gang dressed in leather, mesh, workwear, and smeared makeup saws, drills, sands, and paints pieces of wood into oversized mallets, spears, and toy-like projectiles. Those scenes are intercut with McVety, sporting a yellow mullet and delivering the song from the cold white interior of a van, a knife resting in his hand. Soon, a red-lit pickup carries the crew across the scrub with an enormous handmade slingshot mounted to its bed. Their target is a brightly painted wooden male dummy, equal parts carnival attraction, military mascot, and childhood invention. The friends bombard it with their homemade arsenal before closing in with clubs and axes, collectively demolishing the figure that has been built to represent inherited ideas of manhood. Orange firelight, hard headlights, flying sparks, and icy interior lighting give the desert escapade the character of a pirate raid organized by art-school outcasts. For McVety, the production returned to the reckless ingenuity of childhood while placing that freedom in the hands of his closest creative community: “This video was an absolute labor of love that was entirely done with and by my community of artist friends. I wanted to recapture what it felt like to be a kid when me and my freak friends would make weapons and contraptions and forts inspired by whatever movie we had just seen and often Jack Ass. Whatever felt Rad as Hell then still holds true. We built weapons and made a truck into a giant slingshot. I made a wooden dummy and my friends painted it. It was a party in the desert with the people closest to me.” The video was photographed and co-directed by Adrian Stucker of Melankolia, with Daniel Maggio serving as co-director and editor. It stars Josh McVety, Eli Gray, Matt Hanson, Miranda Sharp, and Eric Runner, with color by Grady Colors. Watch the video for “Victory in Death” below: On creating the video for Victory in Death, Adrian Stucker discusses the film’s high-desert production and the internal conflict represented by its handmade weaponry: “Serving as both Co-Director and Director of Photography for Mellow Code’s “Victory in Death,” I had the opportunity to craft a fantastically fun and highly conceptual visual narrative. The creative direction tied together the rebellious, youthful energy of The Lost Boys with the rugged, weathered aesthetic of desert-faring pirates. Shooting out in the high desert always presents its own unique environmental and logistical challenges, but the cinematic payout is consistently worth the effort. To ground the raw aesthetic of the environment, I frequently utilized a hard, single lighting source, carving out striking, high-contrast imagery against the barren landscape. Drawing directly from Mellow Code’s actual thematic focus on fabricating custom instruments and devices, we wove that maker-centric vibe deeply into the video. The narrative visually documents the meticulous process of crafting tools from other tools, which are eventually forged into weapons. However, the story intentionally subverts the traditional use of these weapons. Instead of directing this arsenal outward at enemies, the weapons are turned inward for a deeply personal fight. The core of the video captures Mellow Code on a mission to confront and metaphorically slaughter his own preconceived notions of masculinity. It is a visual exploration of dismantling internal barriers, illustrating that the most important battles are often fought within ourselves, ultimately making room to replace those outdated notions with the strength and love of the surrounding community.” For Maggio, the concept also provided an opportunity to place McVety’s skills as a carpenter and fabricator directly before the camera: “I love working with Josh. Not only does he make this wonderful, dark, hypnotic music, but he is also a master builder. He’s a brilliant carpenter who can create pretty much anything he designs. The opening shot of FACE IT (the last video we did together) is a handmade illuminated pentagram. He seemed to have made it in his spare time. I was blown away by the detail and its functionality. What can’t this guy do? For the second video, I was curious how far we could push his talents as a craftsman. He runs a shop in Alhambra and naturally works with an extremely talented, fashionable, and hardworking team. Every handmade object featured in the music video was created by the on-camera talent. You can tell they are all friends who share a professional working relationship. One of the highlights was the slingshot mounted to the top of the pickup truck. Our first launch was unsuccessful, and my fondest memory of the shoot was watching 4 cross-faded engineers troubleshoot this thing. I hope it’s as much fun to watch as it was to shoot.” Listen to “Victory in Death” below, and order the single here. Victory In Death by Mellow Code Mellow Code is an avant-garde darkwave project led by Josh McVety and Oliver Michael German. Mechanical rhythms, new-wave vocals, EBM, house, and bright FM synthesis converge with samples gathered from the group’s fabrication workshop. The recent album Object Reality, along with tracks such as “Ich stehe im Blut” and “Face It,” develops an industrial club language in which handmade devices function as instruments, images, and extensions of the music itself. Follow Mellow Code: Facebook Instagram Spotify Bandcamp The post LA Darkwave Project Mellow Code Rebels Against the Machinery of Toxic Masculinity in Video for “Victory in Death” appeared first on Post-Punk.com.

items.body: Band: Genghis Tron | Album: Signal Fire | Genre: Post-metal, Industrial, Cybergrind | Year: 2026 From: Poughkeepsie, USA | Label: Relapse For fans of: Dillinger Escape Plan, Nine Inch Nails, BTBAM Bandcamp Genghis Tron’s last album, 2021’s Dream Weapon, was my introduction to the band. It was also a rather sharp break with their first two records. Where their first two were scourging mixtures of electronica, grindcore, and mathcore, the lush textures and restrained tempos of Dream Weapon were downright relaxing by comparison. Their new album, Signal Fire, then, is something of a return to their earlier sound. It’s not entirely without the spacey post-rock elements that dominate on Dream Weapon, but this is a much more intense and aggressive release. “I Am All” kicks the album off with a staccato synth pattern and a sense of urgency. I’m not nuts about the unclean vocals on stretches of this song. It’s a style common in many genres of metal that end in -core, and that’s simply not something I like. In the context of the music, though, I would consider it an effective choice. I really enjoy the way the textures evolve, gradually becoming more oppressive and anxious. The title track comes next, an upbeat, sub-two-minute piece. There’s a punky, garage rock energy to this song that I love, along with some very fun, unorthodox chords and riffs. Coming straight out of that is “Future Worship”. This piece is more akin to the material on Dream Weapon, but a bit heavier. It’s melodic and synth-fueled, with some beautiful lead guitar lines. “Like Fotochrom” is another short piece, this one centered on looping, echoing synths. After that brief and relaxing interlude, “Tomorrow Mirage” explodes with screams and distorted keys and guitars. Industrial synths buzz harshly over a thumping drum pattern, and the way the band gradually ups the intensity is impressive. The music is furious, desperate, and absolutely crushing. In the song’s second half, things slow down and the piece becomes a mournful bit of electronic rock. “Nothing Blooms in the Hollow” sees the band’s fury come roaring back, this time in a context rooted more in rock and metal, rather than industrial and electronica. Traces of classic space rock acts like Hawkwind are noticeable, and the band does a great job at varying textures and dynamics as this piece progresses. I especially love the percussion in the second half of the song. “Without Form” offers a much-needed breather after that pair of absolutely pummeling compositions. A throbbing synth pulse provides just enough momentum to keep it moving as synth pads bubble in the background. And boy is it good we got that breather, because “Born Prey” pulls no punches in its opening moments, immediately assaulting the listener with black metal-tinged riffage and tortured screams. This mood doesn’t persist for the whole song; things eventually do slow down. The tempo moves from an uncompromising tornado to a steady march driven by growling bass and atmospheric synthesizers. This song becomes increasingly electronic as it progresses, ending up in a beautiful place with multi-part vocal arrangements and relatively warm synth tones. After a brief, relatively calm intro, “A Love So Pure” returns to the band’s cybergrind roots. Mathcore riffs and occasional synth inclusions make for a tense and suffocating experience. The album concludes with “New Gods”. Its opening reminds me of certain Steven Wilson songs, with its moody and minimal electronic backing and cynical lyrics. As it progresses, this song continues to draw melodically from synthpop, albeit in a minor-key and downcast form. Signal Fire, in many ways, is a more mature version of Genghis Tron’s first two records. I don’t particularly like those first two releases (see my above-noted distaste for more “-core” subgenres), so this maturation and diversification of their sound is much-welcomed. Overall, I enjoyed this record more than I expected I would based on the very first moments of it. There’s a clever blend of crushing metal and interstellar synth patterns, as well as some other further-afield inclusions. I still prefer Dream Weapon over this, but it’s pretty solid. Score: 82/100

items.body: UPDATE: the Space Craft festival was canceled Steve Roach had confirmed two live dates for August 2026: “Space Craft” in Joshua Tree, California, on August 14-15, and “Soundquest Festival” in Tucson, Arizona, on August 28-30. Both events place the dark-ambient artist alongside a wider electronic and ambient lineup. The Space Craft is canceled though. Tour dates for Steve Roach August 14-15, 2026 – Space Craft, Pioneertown, Joshua Tree, CA – with Tangerine Dream, ESG, Laraaji, Soriah, Ami Dang, Nailah Hunter and Flore Laurentienne August 28-30, 2026 – Soundquest Festival, La Rosa, Tucson, AZ – with Blood Incantation, Pallbearer, Giuseppe Ottaviani, Soriah, Karima Walker and others Space Craft was a two-night event built around the Perseid meteor shower, combining live performances with stargazing, space talks and storytelling under the night skies of the Mojave Desert. Roach was supposed to perform on the Friday, August 14 bill alongside ESG, Soriah and Ami Dang; Tangerine Dream was to headline the Saturday program with Evicshen. Tickets for Space Craft ranged from $110 to $265. At Soundquest Festival in Tucson, Roach presents “At the Edge of Forever” on Saturday, August 29, preceded by an artist meet-and-greet, and closes the weekend on Sunday, August 30 with a seated set alongside Paul Riedl, Serena Gabriel, Jeff Greinke and Linda Kohanov as part of the festival’s “Sacred Sunday” program. Tickets are available through Eventim and Vivid Seats. About Steve Roach Steve Roach is a California-born, Arizona-based composer working in dark ambient and electronic music since the early 1980s, when albums such as “Structures from Silence” (1984) established the extended, immersive style that has defined his catalogue since. He has released dozens of solo albums on his own Timeroom Editions label and through Projekt Records, alongside collaborations with artists including Vidna Obmana, Robert Rich and Jeffrey Fayman. Side-Line has covered Roach’s recent album and reissue activity, including “The Surface Below” and a reissue of “Stillpoint” (announced November 2025), the archival live collection “The Live Story” with Vidna Obmana (July 2025), a third vinyl edition of “Structures from Silence” (April 2025), and the live album “Crossing the Bridge” (January 2025). Roach also announced a limited 2CD, “La Rosa – Live in Tucson, 2025”, recorded at the same Tucson venue hosting Soundquest Festival this August. The Space Craft and Soundquest Festival dates place Roach on two of the more prominent ambient and electronic live bills of the 2026 season, continuing a year built around reissues, archival releases and festival appearances.

items.body: Lord Of The Lost will reissue “Empyrean” on 18 September 2026 through Out Of Line, marking the tenth anniversary of the German gothic-industrial metal band’s original album. This is a reissue of the 2016 record, not a new studio release. The 10th anniversary edition arrives in two formats. The limited 2LP edition (catalog OUT1551-1552) presses all 13 original tracks in a new remaster onto silver vinyl and adds the bonus track “One World, No Future,” originally released on the “Ruins” EP, a 2018 Sonic Seducer magazine exclusive. The 3CD edition (catalog OUT1548-1550) keeps the original album on disc one and adds two bonus discs: disc two collects rare cuts and alternate versions, including the fan-club-only track “One In A Million,” versions recorded during the COVID-19 lockdown era, a piano version, and one previously unreleased track; disc three carries 12 “Headphone 3D Mixes” of the album’s songs. “Empyrean” was originally released on 29 July 2016 through Out Of Line (catalog OUT 823), the band’s second concept album following “Antagony.” It reached number 9 on the German album charts and was the last Lord Of The Lost studio album released before the band signed to Napalm Records for 2018’s “Judgement.” Out Of Line describes the album’s sound as gothic metal colliding with glam, electro, prog and industrial elements, built around a dystopian, science-fiction narrative about humanity’s search for a promised world called Empyrean. The remastered album tracklist is: Miss Machine Drag Me to Hell The Love of God Raining Stars In Silence Black Oxide (feat. Scarlet Dorn) Interstellar Wars Doomsday Disco Death Penalty No Gods, No War The Interplay of Life and Death Utopya Where Is All the Love One World, No Future (bonus track) Side-Line reviewed “Empyrean” on its original release, praising the album’s mix of heavy guitar work, orchestral arrangements and Chris Harms‘ vocals, and singling out “Miss Machine,” “Doomsday Disco,” “No Gods, No War,” “The Interplay Of Life And Death” and “Utopya” as highlights. The band previously marked another album’s 10th anniversary in 2021 with a reissue of “Antagony,” its 2011 concept album. Lord Of The Lost ‘Empyrean’ bonus material and formats The “Ruins” EP track “One World, No Future,” now added to the 2LP, was originally limited to a Sonic Seducer magazine exclusive release in 2018. The 3CD edition’s second disc gathers material recorded across the album’s touring cycle, including the fan-club track “One In A Million” and lockdown-era recordings, alongside a piano version and one song that has not previously been released. Its third disc applies 12 “Headphone 3D Mixes” to the album’s tracks. About Lord Of The Lost Chris Harms founded Lord Of The Lost in Hamburg, Germany, in mid-2007 as a solo project before recruiting musicians from the city’s music scene to perform the songs live. The band released its debut single, “Dry the Rain,” in 2009, followed by its debut album, “Fears,” in February 2010 through Out Of Line. The second album, “Antagony,” followed in 2011 as the band’s first concept album, and “Die Tomorrow” arrived in 2012. Drummer Tobias Mertens joined in 2014, the same year the band completed its first US tour. In March 2015, Lord Of The Lost released the acoustic album “Swan Songs,” which reached number 34 on the German charts, followed later that year by the “Full Metal Whore” EP. “Empyrean,” the band’s second concept album, followed on 29 July 2016 through Out Of Line, preceded by the single “The Love of God” and the band’s first major European tour, alongside Combichrist and Filter. Guitarist Pi Stoffers and drummer Niklas Kahl joined in 2017, the year the band toured the UK with KMFDM. Lord Of The Lost signed to Napalm Records for 2018’s “Judgement,” continuing with “Judas” (2021), “Weapons of Mass Seduction” (2023) and the “OPVS NOIR” album trilogy released across 2025 and 2026. The band supported Iron Maiden across European tour legs in 2022 and 2023, and represented Germany at the Eurovision Song Contest 2023 with “Blood & Glitter.” The 10th anniversary reissue of “Empyrean” revisits the album that closed out the band’s independent Out Of Line era before its move to Napalm Records.

items.body: Berlin Banter‘s “Indistinct Chatter EP” is now available on green and white vinyl through Instant Noise Productions. The six-track release, which mixes trip hop, electropop and cinematic atmospheres, first came out digitally on May 2, 2025 through the same Berlin-based label. Most of the EP’s tracks are produced and mixed by Mark Saunders, whose credits include mixing work for The Cure and production and mixing work on Tricky’s 1995 debut album “Maxinquaye,” alongside credits for Erasure and a-ha. The track “I Shall Use My Time” features Mark Reeder, the Berlin-based British musician and producer who has lived in the city since 1978 and served as Factory Records’ de facto representative there before founding the electronic label MFS in 1990. “Crystalline” and “Clockwork Orange” both feature Simonne Jones, who sang on Sneaker Pimps‘ 2021 album “Squaring the Circle.” “People Will Unite” features Berlin hip hop artist Yaneq. The EP’s featured single, “I’ll Wait,” brings in Tricky, the Bristol trip hop artist born Adrian Thaws, and is mixed by Gareth Jones, the producer who worked on Depeche Mode’s “Construction Time Again,” “Some Great Reward” and “Black Celebration.” Side-Line previously covered the single’s release in a 2023 article. About Berlin Banter Berlin Banter is an electronic project introduced in 2021 with the five-track cover EP “All Too Familiar,” which reworked tracks by Yazoo, Depeche Mode, The Cure, Pet Shop Boys and Tanita Tikaram. The project returned in 2023 with the original single “I’ll Wait,” featuring Tricky and mixed by Gareth Jones. Berlin Banter released “Indistinct Chatter EP” digitally on May 2, 2025 through Instant Noise Productions, with production and mixing on most tracks by Mark Saunders and collaborations spanning Tricky, Simonne Jones, Mark Reeder and Yaneq. The EP is now also available on green and white vinyl through the label.

items.body: Devoted BJ has released the single Schatten in der Nacht on June 26, 2026, through KL Dark Records. The track moves between dark pop, pop dance, 80s electro and industrial rhythms. “Schatten in der Nacht” is Devoted BJ’s first release since the “Space Time Energy RMX” EP, which came out five years earlier. Two more singles are already in the pipeline, each built around the same blend of dark pop, pop dance, 80s electro and industrial rhythms that has become the artist’s signature sound. KL Dark Records and ‘Schatten in der Nacht’ KL Dark Records describes itself as an artist agency and music label for synth pop, dark pop, dark electro, EBM, body pop, gothic, dark wave and industrial. “Schatten in der Nacht” is available through the label’s Feiyr store page and via Spotify. Side-Line has previously covered the label’s roster, including KL Dark Records launches brand new Neustrohm EP: ‘Red alert’. About Devoted BJ Devoted BJ released the “Space Time Energy RMX” EP five years before “Schatten in der Nacht.” The new single, issued via KL Dark Records on June 26, 2026, marks his return with new electronic material and shows a shift in his songwriting alongside his established sound. Two further singles are planned to follow, each carrying the same mix of dark pop, pop dance, 80s electro and industrial elements. No prior Side-Line coverage of Devoted BJ was found in the archive, and no additional biographical detail beyond the label’s own announcement could be independently verified at the time of writing.

items.body: Glasszone, the coldwave project from Orléans, France, released the four-track EP “Lights” on May 16, 2026. The EP is available on Bandcamp, Spotify, Deezer, iTunes, Amazon Music and YouTube Music. Lights by Glasszone “Lights” runs four tracks: “Lights”, “The Void’s Echo”, “A Strange Feeling” and “Pictures”, all written by Glasszone. The EP carries the coldwave, gothic rock, deathrock, post-punk and shoegaze tags. On the release, Glasszone describes the setting as the misty banks of the Loire, where the project explores a dark and melodic coldwave built from incisive guitars, heavy rhythms and low vocals, moving between melancholy and a quiet tension. Glasszone’s ‘Lights’ EP continues a coldwave catalogue rooted in the Loire The four songs on “Lights” keep to the icy, hypnotic register that has defined Glasszone’s catalogue since its debut, pairing sharp guitar lines with heavier rhythm parts and deep, restrained vocals. About Glasszone Glasszone is a coldwave and post-punk project founded in 2017 in Orléans, on the Loire river in France, self-released and drawing on 80s coldwave with The Cure, Christian Death, Joy Division, Mephisto Walz and Cocteau Twins among its reference points. The project also records as Ex Visio and has issued ten releases between 2018 and 2023, including the albums “Garden of Glass”, “The Other Side”, “Another Dark Place”, “Restless Nights”, “Sleeping Flowers”, “Pictures of the Past”, “Moments” and “To Leave Behind”. “Lights” is Glasszone’s latest EP, released digitally on May 16, 2026.

items.body: Los Angeles darkwave project Mellow Code has released a music video for “Victory in Death,” a track originally issued in October 2025. The video, shot in the high desert, is out now on the band’s own channels. Mellow Code is led by Josh McVety and Oliver Michael German. The project’s sound mixes mechanical rhythms, new-wave vocals, EBM and house with bright FM synthesis, built around samples recorded in the group’s own fabrication workshop in Alhambra, California. “Victory in Death” opens with processional drums and a mass of synthesizers before buzzing, bit-crushed electronics and shuddering samples take over the arrangement. McVety’s vocal sits between lament and command across the track, which addresses masculinity, conditioning and self-erasure. Mellow Code describes the song as one “evoking the feeling of growing up the way American culture targets boys,” adding that the piece was written against “a cycle of abuse” in which “boys police each other and the most conservative minded lash out at the perceived threats to that sense of ‘natural order.'” The accompanying video turns that theme into a nocturnal desert scene. A group dressed in leather, mesh and workwear builds mallets, spears and a truck-mounted slingshot around a campfire, then uses the handmade arsenal to destroy a painted wooden dummy built to represent inherited ideas of manhood. McVety appears throughout, intercut with scenes shot from inside a van. McVety, who also works as a carpenter and fabricator, describes the shoot as a collaboration with his own circle of artists: “This video was an absolute labor of love that was entirely done with and by my community of artist friends. I wanted to recapture what it felt like to be a kid when me and my freak friends would make weapons and contraptions and forts inspired by whatever movie we had just seen and often Jack Ass. We built weapons and made a truck into a giant slingshot. I made a wooden dummy and my friends painted it. It was a party in the desert with the people closest to me.” The video was photographed and co-directed by Adrian Stucker of Melankolia, with Daniel Maggio serving as co-director and editor, and color by Grady Colors. It stars McVety alongside Eli Gray, Matt Hanson, Miranda Sharp and Eric Runner. Stucker describes the shoot’s visual approach as combining “the rebellious, youthful energy of The Lost Boys with the rugged, weathered aesthetic of desert-faring pirates,” noting that a single hard lighting source was used throughout to carve out high-contrast imagery against the desert landscape. “Victory in Death” is streaming on Bandcamp and Spotify. Victory In Death by Mellow Code About Mellow Code Mellow Code is an avant-garde darkwave project led by Los Angeles-based artist Josh McVety together with Oliver Michael German. The project builds its sound from mechanical rhythms, new-wave vocals, EBM and house elements combined with bright FM synthesis, and works samples gathered from McVety’s own fabrication workshop directly into its arrangements, developing an industrial club language in which handmade devices function as instruments as well as imagery. The project’s catalogue includes the album “Objekt Reality” alongside standalone tracks such as “Ich stehe im Blut,” “Face It,” “Antworte” and “Bestraft für Leben,” along with the collaborative track “Knives” with SKM/LKR and the remix “Filed To Knubbs (Male Tears Remix).” “Victory in Death” was released in October 2025 and has now been paired with a video built around the same themes of masculinity and self-imposed conditioning that run through the track, continuing Mellow Code’s pattern of pairing its music with handmade, workshop-built visual production, as seen previously in the video for “Face It.” Mellow Code can be followed on Facebook, Instagram, Spotify and Bandcamp.

items.body: Dead Can Dance released their third studio album, “Within the Realm of a Dying Sun,” on 27 July 1987 through 4AD. The album turns 39 this year. It followed “Spleen and Ideal” (1985), and by the time of its recording the group had narrowed to the core duo of Brendan Perry and Lisa Gerrard, joined by Peter Ulrich on timpani and military snare after members Scott Rodger and James Pinker left the band. The group recorded the album between April and May 1987 at Woodbine studio in Warwickshire, England, produced by Perry, Gerrard and John A. Rivers, with Rivers and Francisco Cabeza engineering. The eight-track album is sequenced across two sides: “Anywhere Out of the World,” “Windfall,” “In the Wake of Adversity” and “Xavier” open the record, followed by “Dawn of the Iconoclast,” “Cantara,” “Summoning of the Muse” and “Persephone (The Gathering of Flowers).” A small ensemble of cello, oboe, trombone, tuba, trumpet, viola and violin players augments the core arrangements, with Gerrard’s vocals featured prominently across the second side. On the album’s expanded instrumentation, the group stated: “We realised we had been limiting our musical visions [before], relying around guitar, bass and drums. These instruments weren’t adequate to express a lot of the things we were hearing.” The cover photograph, taken by Bernard Oudin, shows the grave of French politician and journalist François-Vincent Raspail at the Père-Lachaise cemetery in Paris. “Within the Realm of a Dying Sun” streams on Spotify. About Dead Can Dance Dead Can Dance formed in Melbourne, Australia, in 1981, founded by Brendan Perry and Lisa Gerrard. The duo relocated to London in 1982 and signed to 4AD in 1983, releasing the self-titled debut album “Dead Can Dance” on 27 February 1984. “Spleen and Ideal” followed on 25 November 1985. By the time the group recorded “Within the Realm of a Dying Sun,” members Scott Rodger and James Pinker had left, leaving Gerrard and Perry as the core duo, joined on the album by Peter Ulrich on percussion. 4AD released “Within the Realm of a Dying Sun” on 27 July 1987. It was followed by “The Serpent’s Egg” (1988), “Aion” (1990), “Into the Labyrinth” (1993) and “Spiritchaser” (1996), each record mixing gothic rock, world music and neoclassical elements as Gerrard and Perry’s arrangements grew increasingly orchestral. The band disbanded in 1998 and reunited for the album “Anastasis” in 2012, followed by Dionysus in 2018. Peter Ulrich, who played timpani and military snare on “Within the Realm of a Dying Sun,” has continued to release solo material, including a vinyl reissue of his debut solo album. The anniversary of “Within the Realm of a Dying Sun” places the album back in Dead Can Dance’s timeline as the record that marked the group’s transition to its long-running core duo lineup.

Check it out below. 사루비아 Sarubia by Riff fool About Riff fool Riff fool is a solo electronic artist working out of Seoul, South Korea. The project’s debut album was recorded from December 2021 to May 2025, the period since the artist’s move to Seoul. Beyond his solo work, Riff fool has been active throughout Seoul’s independent music scene, performing live and DJing at local venues including ACS and Channel1969, while also organizing parties and live events in collaboration with artists from diverse creative communities. He is also a resident host on Visla FM, where he presents a regular radio show. He also collaborated with artist Jaeyoung Shin on an visual art presented at SUPERPOP Festival in Japan.

items.body: After several false starts, Zeromancer are finally returning to Germany. The Norwegian industrial-rock band have announced six exclusive headline concerts for February and March 2027 under the banner Testimonial Tour 2027, with Lakeside X joining them as special guests. Zeromancer describe the concerts as their first German shows in eight years. Their last documented appearances in the country took place in Oberhausen and Berlin in November 2019, making the forthcoming run their first return to German stages across eight calendar years. Several earlier attempts to bring Zeromancer back to Germany did not go ahead. A planned Clone Your Lover anniversary concert at Hamburg’s Markthalle was postponed in 2020 while vocalist Alex Møklebust recovered from surgery. The rescheduled performance was eventually cancelled in 2022 after the band reported that its members had been severely affected by COVID-19. Following medical advice, both Zeromancer and Seigmen suspended their live activities for the remainder of that year. More recently, Zeromancer were due to appear at the Unity 2026 events alongside VNV Nation and IAMX. Those concerts were cancelled as VNV Nation’s Ronan Harris underwent a medical procedure addressing severe back pain and required recovery and physiotherapy. The Unity dates could not subsequently be reorganised because of the other bands’ commitments. The newly announced headline tour will now take Zeromancer to six German cities The tour opens on February 26, 2027, in Leipzig and closes on March 13, 2027, in Hamburg. Tickets are available through Eventim Germany. Zeromancer tour dates for 2027 February 26, 2027 – Leipzig, Germany – Täubchenthal February 27, 2027 – Dresden, Germany – Reithalle March 5, 2027 – Frankfurt, Germany – Das Bett March 6, 2027 – Oberhausen, Germany – Kulttempel March 12, 2027 – Berlin, Germany – Columbia Theater March 13, 2027 – Hamburg, Germany – Markthalle About Zeromancer Zeromancer is a Norwegian industrial rock band whose members also play in Seigmen and Ljungblut. The band returned in February 2021 after an eight-year absence with the single “Damned le Monde,” followed by two further EPs the same year, “Mourners” in April and “Terminal Love” in July. The album “Orchestra of Knives” followed in September 2021, described by the band in a Side-Line interview as an album that “differs from previous albums” after the long gap since its predecessor. Member Alex Møklebust has also discussed Seigmen and remixing alongside Apoptygma Berzerk’s Stephan Groth in past Side-Line interviews. “Testimonial Tour 2027” follows the band’s comeback shows earlier in 2026 and marks its return to full headline production in Germany.
